claim: Behavioral inhibition critically relies on frontal cortex - basal ganglia circuits.
source: Flexible behavior requires restraint of actions that are no longer appropriate. This behavioral inhibition critically relies on frontal cortex - basal ganglia circuits.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract without specific data from this study, drawing on general scientific knowledge.

claim: The globus pallidus pars externa (GPe) has been hypothesized to mediate selective proactive inhibition.
source: Within the basal ganglia, the globus pallidus pars externa (GPe) has been hypothesized to mediate selective proactive inhibition: being prepared to stop a specific action, if needed.
evidence: This refers to a hypothesis from prior literature, as indicated by the passive voice 'has been hypothesized'.

claim: Rats selectively engaged proactive inhibition towards specific actions, as shown by slowed reaction times.
source: Rats selectively engaged proactive inhibition towards specific actions, as shown by slowed reaction times (RTs).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript showing RT differences between conditions.

claim: Under proactive inhibition, GPe population activity occupied state-space locations farther from the trajectory followed during normal movement initiation.
source: Under proactive inhibition, GPe population activity occupied state-space locations farther from the trajectory followed during normal movement initiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by neural recording data and state-space analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: State-space locations were predictive of distinct types of errors: failures-to-stop, failures-to-go, and incorrect choices.
source: Furthermore, the state-space locations were predictive of distinct types of errors: failures-to-stop, failures-to-go, and incorrect choices.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neural trajectories associated with different error types shown in the figures.

claim: Slowed RTs on correct proactive trials reflected starting bias towards the alternative action, which was overcome before progressing towards action initiation.
source: Slowed RTs on correct proactive trials reflected starting bias towards the alternative action, which was overcome before progressing towards action initiation.
evidence: This is supported by state-space trajectory analysis showing movement along the Selection axis before the Initiation axis.

claim: Rats can exert cognitive control via strategic adjustments to their GPe network state.
source: Our results demonstrate that rats can exert cognitive control via strategic adjustments to their GPe network state.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the collective findings of the study.

claim: Dysfunctions in behavioral inhibition are involved in many human disorders, including drug addiction.
source: Dysfunctions in behavioral inhibition are involved in many human disorders, including drug addiction (Ersche et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The stop-signal task has been invaluable for revealing specific cortical-basal ganglia mechanisms involved in both movement initiation and inhibition.
source: The stop-signal task has been invaluable for revealing specific cortical-basal ganglia mechanisms involved in both movement initiation ('Going'; e.g. Hanes and Schall, 1996) and inhibition ('Stopping'; e.g. Aron and Poldrack, 2006; Eagle et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Reactive inhibition involves at least two distinct mechanisms: a rapid Pause process mediated via the subthalamic nucleus followed by a Cancel process achieved through pallidostriatal inhibition.
source: 'Reactive' inhibition – making quick use of a Stop cue – appears to involve at least two distinct mechanisms (Schmidt and Berke, 2017): a rapid Pause process mediated via the subthalamic nucleus (STN; Aron and Poldrack, 2006; Schmidt et al., 2013) followed by a Cancel process achieved through pallidostriatal inhibition (Mallet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature including the authors' own work.

claim: Proactive inhibition may be particularly relevant to human life.
source: Proactive inhibition may be particularly relevant to human life (Aron, 2011; Jahanshahi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Reactive inhibition typically involves a global, transient arrest of actions and thoughts.
source: Whereas reactive inhibition typically involves a global, transient arrest of actions and thoughts (Wessel and Aron, 2017), proactive inhibition can be selectively directed to a particular action (Cai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Proactive inhibition can be selectively directed to a particular action.
source: Whereas reactive inhibition typically involves a global, transient arrest of actions and thoughts (Wessel and Aron, 2017), proactive inhibition can be selectively directed to a particular action (Cai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A key behavioral signature of proactive inhibition is slowing of reaction times for that action when the anticipated Stop cue does not actually occur.
source: A key behavioral signature of proactive inhibition is slowing of reaction times (RTs) for that action, when the anticipated Stop cue does not actually occur (e.g. Verbruggen and Logan, 2009; Chikazoe et al., 2009; Zandbelt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some studies have suggested that slowed RTs reflect raising of a decision 'threshold'.
source: In some studies, fitting of models to behavioral data has suggested that slowed RTs reflect raising of a decision 'threshold' (Verbruggen and Logan, 2009; Jahfari et al., 2012), but other studies have found evidence for a slower rate of progression toward threshold instead (Dunovan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Other studies have found evidence for a slower rate of progression toward threshold instead of threshold raising.
source: In some studies, fitting of models to behavioral data has suggested that slowed RTs reflect raising of a decision 'threshold' (Verbruggen and Logan, 2009; Jahfari et al., 2012), but other studies have found evidence for a slower rate of progression toward threshold instead (Dunovan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: It has been proposed that proactive inhibition critically depends on the basal ganglia 'indirect' pathway via GPe.
source: It has been proposed that proactive inhibition critically depends on the basal ganglia 'indirect' pathway via GPe (Aron, 2011; Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Dunovan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Clear support for the hypothesis that proactive inhibition depends on GPe is sparse.
source: Yet clear support for this hypothesis is sparse (Majid et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and represents a gap in knowledge.

claim: There have been few electrophysiological studies of proactive inhibition at the level of individual neurons.
source: There have been few electrophysiological studies of proactive inhibition at the level of individual neurons (Chen et al., 2010; Pouget et al., 2011; Hardung et al., 2017; Yoshida et al., 2018), and to our knowledge none in GPe.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and identifies a gap in the field.

claim: To the authors' knowledge, there have been no electrophysiological studies of proactive inhibition in GPe at the level of individual neurons.
source: There have been few electrophysiological studies of proactive inhibition at the level of individual neurons (Chen et al., 2010; Pouget et al., 2011; Hardung et al., 2017; Yoshida et al., 2018), and to our knowledge none in GPe.
evidence: This is stated as the authors' knowledge of the literature and justifies the novelty of their study.

claim: Analysis of the collective dynamics of motor cortex neurons has provided insights into how brain networks may prepare actions without prematurely triggering them.
source: Analysis of the collective dynamics of motor cortex neurons has provided insights into various aspects of movement control, including how brain networks may prepare actions without prematurely triggering them (Kaufman et al., 2014), and the origins of RT variability (Afshar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Analysis of motor cortex dynamics has provided insights into the origins of RT variability.
source: Analysis of the collective dynamics of motor cortex neurons has provided insights into various aspects of movement control, including how brain networks may prepare actions without prematurely triggering them (Kaufman et al., 2014), and the origins of RT variability (Afshar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Failed Stop trials had similar RTs to the faster part of the Go trial RT distribution.
source: As expected, Failed Stop (error) trials had similar RTs to the faster part of the Go trial RT distribution (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Failures-to-stop typically occur when an underlying Go process evolves more quickly than average.
source: This is consistent with the basic 'race' conceptual model of reactive inhibition (Logan et al., 1984): failures-to-stop typically occur when an underlying Go process evolves more quickly than average (Schmidt et al., 2013), and thus wins the race against a separate Stop process.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and the race model framework.

claim: Median RT for correct contra movements was 251 ms when the Stop cue could not occur (No-Stop).
source: For included sessions, median RT for correct contra movements was 251 ms when the Stop cue could not occur (No-Stop), and 385 ms when the Stop cue could occur (Maybe-Stop) but did not.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data from the study.

claim: Median RT for correct contra movements was 385 ms when the Stop cue could occur (Maybe-Stop) but did not.
source: For included sessions, median RT for correct contra movements was 251 ms when the Stop cue could not occur (No-Stop), and 385 ms when the Stop cue could occur (Maybe-Stop) but did not.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data from the study.

claim: RT slowing due to proactive inhibition was highly selective to the Maybe-Stop direction.
source: RT slowing due to proactive inhibition was highly selective to the Maybe-Stop direction (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; for Maybe-Stop-Contra trials without a Stop cue, median ipsiversive ('ipsi') RT was unslowed at 264 ms).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D and supplementary figures.

claim: For Maybe-Stop-Contra trials without a Stop cue, median ipsiversive RT was unslowed at 264 ms.
source: RT slowing due to proactive inhibition was highly selective to the Maybe-Stop direction (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; for Maybe-Stop-Contra trials without a Stop cue, median ipsiversive ('ipsi') RT was unslowed at 264 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data from the study.

claim: The Maybe-Stop condition was associated with an increase in errors, particularly not responding quickly enough to the Go cue and making the wrong choice.
source: The Maybe-Stop condition was also associated with an increase in errors (Figure 1D), in particular not responding quickly enough to the Go cue that might be followed by Stop (RT limit error; RT >800 ms) and making the wrong choice (incorrect action selection).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 376 GP neurons were recorded from a wide range of GP locations.
source: We recorded individual neurons (n = 376) from a wide range of GP locations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct report of the neural recording data, with anatomical locations shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: GP neurons were tonically-active with a mean session-wide firing rate of 28 Hz.
source: As expected from prior studies (DeLong, 1971; Brotchie et al., 1991; Gardiner and Kitai, 1992; Turner and Anderson, 1997; Arkadir et al., 2004; Gage et al., 2010; Shin and Sommer, 2010; Schmidt et al., 2013; Yoshida and Tanaka, 2016; Mallet et al., 2016) GP neurons were tonically-active (mean session-wide firing rate, 28 Hz) with diverse, complex changes in firing patterns during task performance (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by neural recording data and citations to prior literature.

claim: GP neurons showed diverse, complex changes in firing patterns during task performance.
source: As expected from prior studies (DeLong, 1971; Brotchie et al., 1991; Gardiner and Kitai, 1992; Turner and Anderson, 1997; Arkadir et al., 2004; Gage et al., 2010; Shin and Sommer, 2010; Schmidt et al., 2013; Yoshida and Tanaka, 2016; Mallet et al., 2016) GP neurons were tonically-active (mean session-wide firing rate, 28 Hz) with diverse, complex changes in firing patterns during task performance (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2A and citations to prior literature.

claim: The majority of GP cells showed strongest firing rate changes when activity was aligned relative to movement onset, rather than to the Go or Stop cues.
source: The majority of GP cells showed strongest firing rate changes (increases or decreases) when activity was aligned relative to movement onset, rather than to the Go or Stop cues (Figure 2C,D; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1B for ipsi movement trials).
evidence: This is supported by neural recording data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Individual GP neurons showed greater changes for either contra or ipsi movements, but these were about equally represented in the overall population.
source: Individual neurons showed greater changes for either contra or ipsi movements (Figure 2A,B), but these were about equally represented in the overall population (Figure 2B,E), and the average GP activity was similar for the two movement directions (at least until the movement was already underway; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by neural recording data shown in Figures 2A, 2B, and 2E.

claim: Average GP activity was similar for contra and ipsi movement directions until the movement was already underway.
source: Individual neurons showed greater changes for either contra or ipsi movements (Figure 2A,B), but these were about equally represented in the overall population (Figure 2B,E), and the average GP activity was similar for the two movement directions (at least until the movement was already underway; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: As rats waited for the Go cue, average firing was similar between Maybe-Stop and No-Stop conditions.
source: As rats waited for the (unpredictably-timed) Go cue, average firing was similar between Maybe-Stop and No-Stop conditions (Figure 2F), regardless of whether we examined cells that predominantly increase or decrease activity during movements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2F and supplementary figures.

claim: The fraction of GP cells that fired differently between Maybe-Stop-contra and No-Stop conditions was slightly greater than expected by chance.
source: We did find that the fraction of GP cells that fired differently between these conditions was slightly greater than expected by chance (Figure 2F), consistent with GP involvement in proactive control.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neural recording data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The authors were not able to identify a clear subgroup of individual neurons that strongly and persistently distinguished between Maybe-Stop and No-Stop conditions.
source: However, contrary to our hypothesis, we were not able to identify a clear subgroup of individual neurons that strongly and persistently distinguished between conditions (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the neural recording data analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Proactive control was associated with altered activity in different subsets of GP neurons at various brief moments before the Go cue.
source: Rather, proactive control was associated with altered activity in different subsets of GP neurons at various brief moments before the Go cue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The first 10 principal components together account for 71% of total population variance.
source: For visualization we display the first 3 PCs (which together account for 71% of total population variance; Figure 3B), although statistical analyses used all 10 PCs.
evidence: This is a direct report from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GP state-space trajectories for contra and ipsi movements begin at a similar mean location at the Go cue and diverge gradually until Center Out then rapidly thereafter.
source: Trajectories begin at a similar mean location at the Go cue (diamonds), and diverge gradually until Center Out (large circles) then rapidly thereafter.
evidence: This is supported by the state-space trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: On successful-Stop trials GP activity showed little or no movement before the Stop cue.
source: On successful-Stop trials GP activity showed little or no movement before the Stop cue.
evidence: This is supported by the state-space trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: On failed-Stop trials GP activity was in a significantly different state by the time of the Stop cue, having already evolved a substantial distance along the Initiation Axis.
source: By contrast, on failed-Stop trials GP activity was in a significantly different state by the time of the Stop cue, having already evolved a substantial distance along the Initiation Axis (Figure 3D; includes both contra- and ipsi-cued trials).
evidence: This is supported by the state-space trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Just before the Go cue on Maybe-Stop trials, the GP state was significantly shifted away from action initiation and in the ipsi direction.
source: Just before the Go cue (-100-0ms) the Maybe-Stop state was significantly shifted away from action initiation, and in the ipsi direction.
evidence: This is supported by permutation tests shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Failures to respond quickly enough to the Go cue (RT limit errors) were associated with starting farther away on the Initiation Axis.
source: Failures to respond quickly enough to the Go cue (RT limit errors) were associated with starting farther away on the Initiation Axis (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the state-space trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Incorrect choices (ipsi movements despite contra cue) were associated with starting closer to movement initiation, together with a more-ipsiversive position on the Selection axis at Go cue.
source: By contrast, incorrect choices (ipsi movements despite contra cue) were associated with starting closer to movement initiation, together with a more-ipsiversive position on the Selection axis at Go cue (Figure 4E; Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by the state-space trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Just before the Go cue on Maybe-Stop trials, rats showed no difference on the Initiation Axis but were significantly shifted on the Selection axis, in the ipsiversive direction.
source: Just before the Go cue on Maybe-Stop trials, rats showed no difference on the Initiation axis but were significantly shifted on the Selection Axis, in the ipsiversive direction (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by permutation tests shown in Figure 5B.

claim: After the Go Cue, movement on the Initiation axis was delayed compared to No-Stop trials, but movement on the Selection Axis occurred earlier.
source: After the Go Cue, movement on the Initiation axis was delayed compared to No-Stop trials, but movement on the Selection Axis occurred earlier (Figure 5C; Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by the trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: On correctly-performed Maybe-Stop trials the GP network engaged a dynamical sequence that was not observed on No-Stop trials: they first overcame a proactive bias towards the alternative action, before proceeding to initiate the action that had been cued.
source: Thus, on correctly-performed Maybe-Stop trials the GP network engaged a dynamical sequence that was not observed on No-Stop trials: they first overcame a proactive bias towards the alternative action, before proceeding to initiate the action that had been cued.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the trajectory data showing sequential movement along Selection then Initiation axes.

claim: Comparing Maybe-Stop trials with No-Stop trials with the same RT (RT-matching) showed different positions on the Selection Axis at Go cue.
source: Comparing Maybe-Stop trials with No-Stop trials with the same RT (RT-matching) again showed different positions on the Selection Axis at Go cue (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-matched trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The difference in Selection Axis position was not seen when comparing slower and faster RTs within the No-Stop condition.
source: This difference was not seen when comparing slower and faster RTs within the No-Stop condition (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Spontaneously-slower RTs appeared to arise through slower evolution along both Initiation and Selection Axes simultaneously.
source: Rather, spontaneously-slower RTs appeared to arise through slower evolution along both Initiation and Selection Axes simultaneously (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: On Maybe-Stop trials movement along the Selection axis overshot the level reached on No-Stop trials.
source: Furthermore, on Maybe-Stop trials movement along the Selection axis overshot the level reached on No-Stop trials, as if overcompensating for the initial bias on this axis (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claim: The overshoot on the Selection axis was not seen for spontaneously-slower No-Stop trials.
source: This overshoot was not seen for spontaneously-slower No-Stop trials (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Variation in RT reflects multiple dynamic processes within basal ganglia circuits, with slowing due to proactive inhibition involving distinct internal control mechanisms to spontaneous RT variation.
source: We conclude that variation in RT reflects multiple dynamic processes within basal ganglia circuits, with slowing due to proactive inhibition involving distinct internal control mechanisms to spontaneous RT variation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative trajectory analyses.

claim: Repeating key analyses within the full 376-dimensional state space produced essentially identical trajectory differences between conditions.
source: We therefore repeated key analyses within the full 376-dimensional state space. Defining Initiation and Selection Axes in the same way as before, but without the PCA step, produced essentially identical trajectory differences between conditions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the control analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: A key behavioral signature of proactive control – selective slowing of RTs when a Stop signal is expected - can arise through multiple covert strategies.
source: We have demonstrated here that a key behavioral signature of proactive control – selective slowing of RTs when a Stop signal is expected - can arise through multiple covert strategies.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the behavioral and neural data.

claim: Multiple covert strategies for proactive control are visible as changes to the dynamic state of GPe by the time of Go cue presentation.
source: These are visible as changes to the dynamic state of GPe by the time of Go cue presentation, and include a bias towards an alternative action, and/or starting further from the 'point-of-no-return' in action initiation.
evidence: This is supported by the state-space trajectory analyses showing different starting positions.

claim: Which internal strategies are employed for proactive inhibition is likely influenced by the specific experimental conditions.
source: Which internal strategies are employed for proactive inhibition is likely influenced by the specific experimental conditions (Mayse et al., 2014; Yoshida et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The brief limited hold period (800 ms) may have led rats to sometimes make guesses as to which cues will be presented, and position their neural state accordingly.
source: For example, we used a brief limited hold period (800 ms) to encourage subjects to respond rapidly to the Go cue rather than waiting to see if the Stop cue is presented. This time pressure may have led rats to sometimes make guesses as to which cues will be presented, and position their neural state accordingly.
evidence: This is speculation about how task design may have influenced behavior.

claim: The ipsi bias observed on the Selection axis on Maybe-Stop (contra) trials may partly reflect asymmetric reward expectancy.
source: Motivational aspects are known to be important in proactive inhibition (Meyer and Bucci, 2016): the ipsi bias we observed on the Selection axis on Maybe-Stop (contra) trials may partly reflect asymmetric reward expectancy (Kawagoe et al., 1998), simply because ipsi movements are more consistently rewarded from that state.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior literature on motivation and reward.

claim: Rats are unable to consistently select from the slower portion of their regular RT distribution, given the high spontaneous variability in RTs.
source: It might seem simpler, and less error-prone, for the rats to just select from the slower portion of their regular RT distribution. We suggest that they are unable to consistently do so, given the high spontaneous variability in RTs.
evidence: This is speculation about why rats use the observed strategies.

claim: The degree to which specific neural strategies are employed may vary between rats.
source: The degree to which specific neural strategies are employed may also vary between rats; we found some preliminary evidence for this (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), though investigating this further would require more animals and more recorded cells in each animal.
evidence: This is supported by preliminary data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rats did slow down slightly on average after Stop trials or errors.
source: Although not the focus of this study, our rats did slow down slightly on average after Stop trials or errors (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Slowing after Stop trials or errors was associated with a modest shift on the Initiation Axis in the same, movement-opposed direction as in the main results, but this effect did not reach significance.
source: This slowing was associated with a modest shift on the Initiation Axis in the same, movement-opposed direction as in our main results (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), but this effect did not reach significance.
evidence: This is supported by neural data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Both behavioral and neural data suggest that the cued component of proactive inhibition was substantially greater than post-trial adjustments under the particular task conditions used.
source: Thus both behavioral and neural data suggest that the cued component of proactive inhibition was substantially greater than post-trial adjustments under our particular task conditions.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral and neural data comparing cued and post-trial effects.

claim: The ability to reveal distinct strategies for proactive inhibition relies on a dynamical systems approach with single-cell resolution.
source: Our ability to reveal distinct strategies for proactive inhibition relies on a dynamical systems approach with single-cell resolution.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion drawn from the study's approach.

claim: The dynamical systems method may be especially important for deciphering structures like GP, where projection neurons show continuous, diverse activity patterns.
source: This method may be especially important for deciphering structures like GP, where projection neurons show continuous, diverse activity patterns.
evidence: This is speculation about the importance of the method based on the characteristics of GP neurons.

claim: As intermingled GP neurons increased and decreased firing at each moment, the resulting network state changes would likely be undetected using aggregate measures such as photometry or fMRI.
source: As intermingled GP neurons increased and decreased firing at each moment, the resulting network state changes would likely be undetected using aggregate measures such as photometry or fMRI.
evidence: This is speculation about the limitations of other methods based on the observed diversity of GP neuron responses.

claim: An enhanced ability to make subtle adjustments to dynamical state may be part of the reason why GP projection neurons show high spontaneous activity.
source: Speculatively, we suggest that an enhanced ability to make subtle adjustments to dynamical state may be part of the reason why GP projection neurons show high spontaneous activity, in contrast to (for example) the near-silence of most striatal projection neurons, most of the time.
evidence: This is explicitly labeled as speculation about the functional significance of GP neuron properties.

claim: Prior examinations of motor/premotor cortical dynamics during reaching movements in non-human primates have demonstrated distinct neural dimensions for movement preparation and execution ('What' to do) and movement triggering ('When' to do it).
source: Prior examinations of motor/premotor cortical dynamics during reaching movements in non-human primates have demonstrated distinct neural dimensions for movement preparation and execution ('What' to do) and movement triggering ('When' to do it) (Elsayed et al., 2016; Kaufman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The Selection and Initiation axes in this study are analogous to the 'What' and 'When' dimensions in prior primate studies.
source: Our Selection and Initiation axes are analogous, although our task lacks an explicit preparation epoch and has only two action choices (left vs. right).
evidence: This is an inference comparing the current findings to prior literature.

claim: In non-human primate studies, movement preparation occurred in distinct, orthogonal dimensions to movement execution, whereas in this study preparatory 'bias' was along the same Selection axis that differentiated ipsi and contra trajectories during movement itself.
source: One notable difference in the non-human primate studies is that movement preparation occurred in distinct, orthogonal dimensions to movement execution, whereas we saw preparatory 'bias' along the same Selection axis that differentiated ipsi and contra trajectories during movement itself.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current findings and prior literature.

claim: The observation that on correct Maybe-Stop trials, GP state evolved first along the Selection axis is consistent with evidence that movement preparation and movement initiation can be independent processes.
source: Nonetheless, our observation that on correct Maybe-Stop trials, GP state evolved first along the Selection axis is consistent with evidence that movement preparation and movement initiation can be independent processes (Haith et al., 2016; Thura and Cisek, 2017), and that these can be differentially modulated by the basal ganglia and dopamine (Leventhal et al., 2014; Manohar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and the current data.

claim: The current findings appear consistent with recent observations that, following an unexpected late change in target location, preparation dimensions are rapidly re-engaged.
source: It also appears consistent with recent observations that, following an unexpected late change in target location, preparation dimensions are rapidly re-engaged (Ames et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and comparison to current findings.

claim: The distinction between What and When dimensions is not readily compatible with sequential-sampling mathematical models of decision-making.
source: The distinction between What and When dimensions is not readily compatible with sequential-sampling mathematical models of decision-making (Smith and Ratcliff, 2004; Brown and Heathcote, 2008; Noorani and Carpenter, 2016), which typically assume that RTs (When) directly reflect sufficient accumulation of evidence for a particular choice (What).
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings for theoretical models, supported by citations.

claim: When sensory cues are unambiguous the selection process appears to be much faster than standard RTs.
source: Furthermore, when sensory cues are unambiguous the selection process appears to be much faster than standard RTs (Stanford et al., 2010; Haith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Why RTs are typically so much slower and more variable than required for sensory processing or action selection is not fully clear, but this extra time provides opportunity for impulsive or inappropriate responses to be overruled, to increase behavioral flexibility.
source: Why RTs are typically so much slower and more variable than required for sensory processing or action selection is not fully clear, but this extra time provides opportunity for impulsive or inappropriate responses to be overruled, to increase behavioral flexibility.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of RT variability.

claim: The GPe is well positioned to contribute to behavioral control.
source: The GPe is well positioned to contribute to such behavioral control.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of GPe connectivity and function.

claim: GPe has bidirectional connections with the subthalamic nucleus, a key component of the 'hyperdirect' pathway from frontal cortex that slows decision-making under conditions of conflict.
source: GPe has bidirectional connections with the subthalamic nucleus, a key component of the 'hyperdirect' pathway from frontal cortex that slows decision-making under conditions of conflict (Cavanagh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: GPe itself is the target of the 'indirect' (striatopallidal) pathway, believed to discourage action initiation ('NoGo').
source: GPe itself is the target of the 'indirect' (striatopallidal) pathway, believed to discourage action initiation ('NoGo'; Yoshida and Tanaka, 2016; Kravitz et al., 2010), possibly due to pessimistic predictions of reward (Collins and Frank, 2014; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In standard, firing rate-based models of basal ganglia function, GPe activity restrains actions by preventing pauses in the firing of basal ganglia output.
source: In standard, firing rate-based models of basal ganglia function, GPe activity restrains actions by preventing pauses in the firing of basal ganglia output, that are in turn required to disinhibit movement-related activity in the brainstem and elsewhere (Chevalier and Deniau, 1990; Roseberry et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature describing standard models.

claim: The standard firing rate-based model of basal ganglia function is too simple.
source: However, it is well-recognized that this model is too simple (Gurney et al., 2001; Klaus et al., 2019), and it does not account for the complex activity patterns within GPe that we and others have observed.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and the current observations.

claim: A straightforward application of the rate model might predict a systematic decrease in GPe firing rate with proactive inhibition, but this was not observed.
source: For example, a straightforward application of the rate model might predict a systematic decrease in GPe firing rate with proactive inhibition, but we did not observe this (Figure 2), with the possible exception of trials with RT limit errors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the neural data that contradicts predictions from standard models.

claim: Examining dimension-reduced population dynamics is a promising alternative approach for deciphering how subtle modulations in the firing of many basal ganglia neurons are coordinated to achieve behavioral functions.
source: Based on the current results, examining dimension-reduced population dynamics is a promising alternative approach for deciphering how subtle modulations in the firing of many basal ganglia neurons are coordinated to achieve behavioral functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion about methodological implications based on the study's findings.

claim: The study did not record large populations of neurons simultaneously, which precludes effective analysis of neural dynamics on individual trials.
source: We did not record large populations of neurons simultaneously, which precludes effective analysis of neural dynamics on individual trials (Afshar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study.

claim: The study did not classify GPe neurons by projection target largely because sleep data was not consistently recorded.
source: We did not classify GPe neurons by projection target (Mallet et al., 2016; Abecassis et al., 2020) largely because we did not consistently record sleep data to enable that classification (Mallet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study.

claim: It is not yet known the extent to which these population dynamics are shared with upstream and downstream structures.
source: We do not yet know the extent to which these population dynamics are shared with upstream (e.g. striatum) and downstream (e.g. substantia nigra pars reticulata) structures, which will be essential for elucidating how these dynamic changes actually influence behavior.
evidence: This is a stated limitation and direction for future research.

claim: It has not yet been determined how the population dynamics reported here relate to oscillatory dynamics reported in cortical-basal ganglia circuits during movement suppression and in pathological states.
source: Finally, we have not yet determined how the population dynamics reported here relate (if at all) to oscillatory dynamics reported in cortical-basal ganglia circuits during movement suppression (Swann et al., 2009; Cavanagh et al., 2011; Leventhal et al., 2012) and in pathological states such as Parkinson's Disease (Hammond et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a stated limitation and direction for future research, with citations to relevant prior work.

claim: Approximately half of rats that began learning the task variant acquired clear proactive inhibition within 3 months of training.
source: Among rats that began learning this task variant, approximately half acquired clear proactive inhibition within 3 months of training (see Materials and methods), and were thus considered eligible for electrode implantation.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral training outcomes.

claim: 63 behavioral sessions with a significant proactive inhibition effect and distinct GP single units (n = 376 neurons) were selected for further analysis.
source: We selected for further analysis those behavioral sessions (n = 63) with a significant proactive inhibition effect (i.e. longer RT when a Stop cue might occur; one-tail Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.05) and distinct GP single units (n = 376 neurons included).
evidence: This is a direct report of the data selection criteria and sample size.

claim: Prior work has shown particular basal ganglia involvement in the control of contraversive orienting-type movements.
source: Prior work has shown particular basal ganglia involvement in the control of contraversive orienting-type movements (i.e. directed towards the opposite side; Carli et al., 1985; Isoda and Hikosaka, 2008; Schmidt et al., 2013; Leventhal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The study focused on proactive control of movements contraversive to the recorded cell locations.
source: We therefore focused on proactive control of movements contraversive ('contra') to the recorded cell locations; for example we included a left GPe cell only if the rat demonstrated proactive control for rightward movements during that recording session.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methodological approach.

claim: Change along both Initiation and Selection axes was not dominated by a small proportion of GP neurons, but instead there were smaller contributions from many individual cells located throughout GP.
source: Along both Initiation and Selection axes, change was not dominated by a small proportion of GP neurons. Instead, there were smaller contributions from many individual cells located throughout GP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1AC-E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neuron weights shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Within state space, population activity was very similar for contra and ipsi movements at the Go cue.
source: Within state space, population activity was very similar for contra and ipsi movements at the Go cue (Figure 3C), and initially evolved in a common direction before progressively separating into distinct trajectories (Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by state-space trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: GP population activity initially evolved in a common direction before progressively separating into distinct trajectories for contra and ipsi movements.
source: Within state space, population activity was very similar for contra and ipsi movements at the Go cue (Figure 3C), and initially evolved in a common direction before progressively separating into distinct trajectories (Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by state-space trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3C and Video 1.

claim: On Maybe-Stop trials movement along the Selection axis overshot the level reached on No-Stop trials, as if overcompensating for the initial bias on this axis.
source: Furthermore, on Maybe-Stop trials movement along the Selection axis overshot the level reached on No-Stop trials, as if overcompensating for the initial bias on this axis (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory data, with the 'as if' phrase indicating an interpretation.

claim: The tail of the Failed-Stop distribution (RT >500 ms) is presumed to reflect trials for which rats successfully responded to the Stop cue, but then failed to maintain holding until reward delivery.
source: The tail of the Failed-Stop distribution (RT >500 ms) is presumed to reflect trials for which rats successfully responded to the Stop cue, but then failed to maintain holding until reward delivery (see Leventhal et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2013; Mayse et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Failed-Stop trials with RT >500 ms were excluded from electrophysiological analyses.
source: Failed-Stop trials with RT >500 ms were excluded from electrophysiological analyses, since these were presumed to reflect trials for which rats successfully responded to the Stop cue, but then failed to maintain holding until reward delivery (see Leventhal et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2013; Mayse et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data analysis approach.

claim: For included sessions, the median number of Go trials was 266 (range, 167–361) and the median number of Stop trials was 57 (range, 27–95).
source: For included sessions, the median number of Go trials was 266 (range, 167–361) and the median number of Stop trials was 57 (range, 27–95).
evidence: This is a direct report of the sample sizes in the study.
